name: Mathseeds
line: Mathseeds places a child, then moves lesson by lesson. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Mathseeds: Mathseeds places a child, then moves lesson by lesson. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Mathseeds sets a starting point with a placement test, then moves a child lesson by lesson, with a quiz at the end of each map of five lessons [2][3]. In AMP, the problem is the unit. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after that updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem. Mathseeds sets the starting point with a placement test [3]. After that a child moves lesson by lesson, and any lesson can be repeated [2].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem in front of the learner: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Mathseeds the unit is the lesson: a short animated scene, nine activities, then an e-book the child reads or hears narrated [2]. A meta-analysis of 55 studies found that worked examples improve math performance [14].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts as learned when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. An answer after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In Mathseeds, five lessons make a map, and the map ends in a quiz [2]. The company says its Driving Tests and end-of-map quizzes make sure children reach mastery [2]. We found no stated rule for what counts as mastery [2][5]. AMP's rule is open source: open to peer review and contribution.

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Mathseeds' white paper describes a spiral: early concepts are revisited in later lessons of the course [5]. We found no review timed to each child's own answers in its published materials [2][5]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [13].

reasons.title: One program past grade 3
reasons.body: AMP runs from counting through precalculus in one program, on one map of skills, and keeps a separate level for each part of math. A learner further along in one part than another gets work at both levels. Mathseeds is built for ages 3 to 9 and covers kindergarten through grade 3 in schools [1][4].

rows.range: Ages 3 to 9 at home. Kindergarten through grade 3 in schools [1][4].
rows.start: A placement test sets the starting lesson [3].
rows.teaching: In the lesson: short animated scenes with cartoon characters, nine activities, then an e-book the child reads or hears narrated [2][5].
rows.next: The next lesson in the sequence. Any lesson can be repeated [2].
rows.mastery: Driving Tests, and a quiz at the end of each map of five lessons [2][5].
rows.review: A spiral by design: early concepts come back in later lessons [5].
rows.print: Printable worksheets [3]. Print workbooks for kindergarten to grade 2 that match the online lessons, the same pages for every child [9].
rows.adult: Light. Progress reports and printables, and 36-week guides for adults who want to teach alongside it [3].
rows.reports: Progress reports for families [3]. Real-time reports and automated scoring for schools [4].
rows.evidence: A study contracted by 3P Learning: grade 3 users g = 0.14 above 100 non-users in one district [6]. No Evidence for ESSA rating [12].

theirs: Mathseeds is an online math program for children aged 3 to 9 [1]. Schools use it for kindergarten through grade 3 [4]. Blake eLearning develops it [7], and 3P Learning lists it among its products beside Reading Eggs and Mathletics [10].

A placement test sets where a child starts [3]. A lesson opens with a short animated scene featuring one of its cartoon characters. Nine activities follow, then an e-book the child can read or hear narrated. Finishing a lesson hatches a pet. Five lessons make a map, which ends in a quiz and a printable certificate [2].
credit: Built for the youngest learners, from age 3, with e-books a child can hear read aloud [1][2].
Concrete before abstract: grouping and number lines come before written methods [5].
It has published studies with comparison groups [6][7].

theirs: Mathseeds' main study was run by LearnPlatform under contract to 3P Learning [6]. It covers 2021-22 in ten elementary schools in one southeastern U.S. district. In grade 3, 605 users were compared with 100 students who did not use Mathseeds, adjusting for fall scores, without random assignment. Users scored higher on NWEA MAP in the spring, by g = 0.14, with mean scores of 199 against 197 [6]. In kindergarten through grade 2 the report compared students who completed many lessons (35 to 110) with students who completed few (0 to 13): g = 0.08 across those grades, significant in grade 1 and not in kindergarten or grade 2 [6]. Students who complete many lessons can differ from those who complete few before they start. The company calls this ESSA Level II evidence [8].

An earlier kindergarten study, The Mathseeds Effect (2015-16), by SEG Measurement and MarketingWorks, compared 125 Mathseeds students with 192 others in six states and reported an effect of 0.48 on the SESAT 1 math test. It compared classes without random assignment, and its page does not say who paid for it. Mathseeds classes were included only if they averaged at least 14 completed lessons per student [7]. A 2019-20 case study of one Pennsylvania school reports 1.1 grade levels of progress, with no comparison group and without naming the measure [11].
Evidence for ESSA lists Mathseeds without a rating: "No studies met inclusion requirements" [12].
ours: Two findings bear most on this comparison. A meta-analysis of 55 studies found that worked examples improve math performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 [14]. The studies run from elementary school to college, and most use researcher-designed tests. In a randomized trial that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks a month later, on the researchers' own test [13]. AMP applies both.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: Your child is three to five and you want characters, stories and narrated books.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice, mixed with other math.
Your child is at different levels in different parts of math, or ready for work past grade 3.
You want printed workbooks made from your child's own record.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Mathseeds?
questions.answer: Mathseeds places a child with a test, then moves lesson by lesson, with a quiz at the end of each map [2][3]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Mathseeds work?
questions.answer: A study LearnPlatform ran for 3P Learning found grade 3 users scored g = 0.14 higher than 100 non-users in one district, without random assignment [6]. Evidence for ESSA lists Mathseeds without a rating [12].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs, and AMP places a learner from their first answers.
